newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania opposition triumphs over ruling leftists.
newsitem.headline: Romania opposition triumphs over ruling leftists.

text.p: Romania's centrist opposition has surged to victory in parliamentary elections, deposing ex-communists in power since 1989, but the race for the presidency remained wide open on Monday.

Emil Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR), which calls for faster reforms to drag Romania out of economic decline, secured a central role in the next governing coalition by opening up a big lead in both houses of parliament.
It will be the first taste of power for the anti-communist opposition in Romania.

In the parliamentary poll, the CDR won just over 30 percent of votes for the lower Chamber of Deputies, routing President Ion Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) with 22 percent. Official figures for the Senate were roughly similar.

But Iliescu's personal fate was uncertain. With about half the votes counted in the presidential race, Iliescu had 33 percent backing, five ahead of Constantinescu. The two leaders now contest a November 17 run-off.
International observers pronounced the vote fair.
Analysts warned that a CDR-led government would have to abandon populist promises and take unpopular measures to kick-start the weak Romanian economy.

"It will have to be a government of sacrifice whose successes will be judged according to the extent to which they manage to secure solid change even if social costs are high," independent economist Ilie Serbanescu told Reuters.
"The new government will have to rebalance the economy by restructuring, allowing prices to rise and accepting a further depreciation of the leu."

The Convention advocates a "contract with Romania" -- an ambitious plan to speed reforms. It commits a CDR government to quitting within 200 days if it fails to raise living standards and upgrade farming and industry.
Campaign teams retreated from view after the vote to consider coalition options and plan for the next round.

Iliescu looked dejected as exit polls made clear the extent of his party's debacle. But official results have proved better and his advantage was likely to increase as results come in from remote rural areas which normally support him.
Stelian Tanase, an independent analyst, said the CDR win would enhance the country's standing abroad.
"Romania's prestige and foreign image will be very much enhanced by this outcome," said Tanase. "Romania had been regarded as the poor sister of east European reform."
But it was not entirely clear which partners would form a governing coalition or how Iliescu might work with a hostile parliament if he held on to win the run-off.
The CDR's most logical partner is ex-premier Petre Roman's Social Democratic Union (USD), which has a broadly similar reformist programme.
Cooperation between the two parties has been hampered by a personality clash and Roman made no promises on election night.
Iliescu tried to exploit opposition differences by suggesting the CDR might be better off building a coalition with his battered PDSR. But the CDR and USD rule that out.
Of other parties clearing the three percent barrier to enter parliament, the ethnic Hungarian UDMR party is the largest with six percent. It is generally hostile to Iliescu.
